items.title: George Wein interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: my brother knew Red Allen and J.C. Higginbotham and I’d sit in with them

ctx.x: They petered out and I wanted to learn how to play popular so I could — I don’t know why, I didn’t think of myself as a singer — but I liked to play and sing and so I wanted to accompany myself instead of having my mother accompany. Because I just sang at parties in the house, “Georgie you’ve got to sing a song, Georgie you’ve got to sing a song, Georgie you’ve got to sing a song.” And I don’t want to give you the impression I was a good singer, but I was a kid that could sing a song and I wasn’t any boy wonder.…

cellar at the house we had in Newton, Massachusetts, and I found four saxophones and two trombones and three trumpets and piano, bass — I was the piano player. I went out and bought stock arrangements, we all bought them. And my mother knew somebody from New York and I went down there, we took a trip, I got free arrangements from the publishers. Just like a kid has a rock & roll band, in those days I had a dance band. We used to play Tommy Dorsey’s “Song of India” and Glenn Miller’s “In the Mood” and Erskine…

Isn’t that interesting. You know I have to remind myself, when you talk about some of those tunes you were playing with your first band, they sound old but for you guys, that was the current music of the day, is that right?

items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I brought up Wild Bill Davison and Frankie Newton and J.C. [Higginbotham] from New York, and we sold out Jordan Hall in Boston.

ctx.x: Was that the Brass Bands to BeBop?

Brass Bands to BeBop. Nat Hentoff wrote the album notes and MC'd the program. I brought up Wild Bill Davison and Frankie Newton and J.C. [Higginbotham] from New York, and we sold out Jordan Hall in Boston. Beautiful hall … at the New England Conservatory of Music. I guess that was the first bite of the insect that infected me the rest of my life.

items.title: 67247_J.C. Higginbotham oral history interview
items.q: I just liked him that much, he and his whole family. I just felt like I was in the family.

ctx.x: How do you mean didn't charge him nothing?

I just liked him that much, he and his whole family. I just felt like I was in the family. The last time I played in his house Mary Lou Williams was out there. Boy, it was cold, not c-o-l-d but k-o-l-d. So after we finished working we went out... That was the last time I went out there. I saw Mary Lou a couple of times...
After you did the record in Atlanta and you came to New York and you went back down to Atlanta to work on a steady job. Where was the place you were working in Atlanta on a steady job?
